title.en: Formic acid and the red ants

text.en: Formic acid got its name from Formica, the Latin word for red ants, because it was first obtained from them. As thousands of organic compounds were discovered, such source-based names became impossible to manage, so scientists made a system of naming by structure.

A homologous series is a group of organic compounds with the same general formula and similar chemical properties, in which successive members differ by a CH2 group.
Look at the alkanes: methane CH4, ethane CH3CH3, propane CH3CH2CH3, butane CH3(CH2)2CH3 and pentane CH3(CH2)3CH3, each with one more CH2 than the one before.
Each member differs from the next by one methylene group, which means a difference of 14 amu in molecular mass.
All members of a series contain the same elements and the same functional group, and they are represented by one general formula, such as CnH2n+2 for alkanes.
Their physical properties change regularly with increasing molecular mass, their chemical properties are similar, and they can be prepared by a common method.
In ancient days names came from natural sources, as formic acid came from red ants, but later compounds were made from other sources, so a systematic method of naming was needed.
IUPAC, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, framed the rules for naming organic compounds by their structure.
An IUPAC name has three parts, written in this order: prefix, root word and suffix.
The root word tells the number of carbon atoms in the parent chain: Meth 1, Eth 2, Prop 3, But 4, Pent 5, Hex 6, Hept 7, Oct 8, Non 9 and Dec 10.
The prefix shows the substituents or branches, which are atoms or groups other than hydrogen attached to the parent chain.
The suffix shows the type of bonding or the functional group, such as -ane for single bonds, -ene for a double bond, -yne for a triple bond and -ol for the alcohol group.
So CH3CH2CH3 has three carbons, root Prop, and single bonds, suffix -ane, giving propane, while CH3CH2OH has two carbons and an -OH group, giving ethanol.

problem.en: Give the IUPAC name of a straight-chain compound with 4 carbon atoms and a C=C double bond, and write its formula.

text.en: Four carbons give the root word But.
A double bond gives the suffix -ene, so the name is butene.
Alkenes follow CnH2n, so with n = 4 the formula is C4H8.

why.en: Use the general formula for the series.

prompt.en: Explain what a homologous series is and how an IUPAC name is built.

requiredIdeas.en: Same general formula, successive members differ by CH2
Root word gives the number of carbons

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking members differ by one carbon and two hydrogens in different ways
Mixing up the prefix and the suffix

points.en: Homologous series: same functional group and general formula; successive members differ by CH2 (14 amu).
IUPAC name = prefix + root word + suffix.
Root words: Meth, Eth, Prop, But, Pent, Hex, Hept, Oct, Non, Dec for 1 to 10 carbons.
Physical properties change regularly along the series; chemical properties stay similar.
